newsitem.title: USA: Boeing not backing down from sole-supplier deals.
newsitem.headline: Boeing not backing down from sole-supplier deals.

text.p: Continental Airlines Inc.'s announcement Tuesday that it will turn to Boeing Co. for all its new jets over the next 20 years comes as a stinging rebuke to European officials who have assailed such pacts.

The long-expected deal, including an initial order for 35 wide-body jets valued at $3 billion, was announced two days before the European Commission opens a hearing on Boeing's plan to acquire McDonnell Douglas Corp. that is expected to focus on such exclusive supplier arrangements.

Boeing executives said they had nothing to do with the timing of Continental's announcement but adamantly defended the deal, which helped drive Boeing stock up $1.25 to a record $57.25 in active consolidated New York Stock Exchange afternoon trading.
"Basically, we had an airplane competition, and it was a very public one," said Boeing spokeswoman Liz Verdier. "We don't win them all."
David Venz, a spokesman for Boeing's European rival Airbus Industrie, expressed disappointment over the deal and criticised Boeing's exclusive arrangement pacts.

"Clearly this has the appearance of Boeing making a grab at locking up the American market," Venz said. "It's our position that these exclusive deals are anti-competitive and that they are just bad for this industry."

Analysts said they saw the Continental deal as a clear sign the world's biggest airplane manufacturer has no intention of backing down in the face of threats the European Commission will try to derail the proposed $14 billion McDonnell Douglas merger.

"I think it's pretty clear that Boeing's not making any real attempt to be very conciliatory in this whole process with the (European Union)," said analyst Jack Modzelewski of PaineWebber. "Maybe Boeing's taking the hardest line possible so it won't have to concede much."
He and other analysts said they expected the merger to be approved by both European and U.S. authorities in time for an expected August close.

Several analysts suggested Boeing might agree not to pursue any more exclusive-supplier deals now that it has wrapped up three of the world's biggest carriers in AMR Corp.'s American Airlines, Delta Air Lines Inc. and now Continental.

"They probably are going to have to do something," said Paul Nisbet of JSA Research. "The alternative is going to be a trade war, and the U.S. government is letting the EU be well aware that it is backing Boeing."

Boeing executive Jerry King, who is in charge of the company's nmerger transition team, and commercial airplane group Executive Vice President Dick Albrecht go before the EC Thursday to respond to a 40-page "statement of objections" to the merger issued by the commission last month.
European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert has made it clear that the exclusive-supplier contracts are his No. 1 concern.

"Boeing's position will be to point out that the merger won't affect competiiton with Airbus," company spokeswoman Sherry Nebel said. "Boeing also will stress that the buying power of airlines will continue to insure vigorous competition between Boeing and Airbus for commercial airplane orders."

The two-day hearing is closed to the public but open to interested parties such as Airbus representatives. The commission is expected to forward a draft decision to the EU's 15 member countries by mid-July in time for a final decision by the end of the month.
